subject: Huawei now outsells Nvidia in China, on 4% of the compute
bodyMarkdown:
Huawei says it has passed Nvidia in China's AI chip market, and if you hold an S&P 500 index fund in your RRSP you own a slice of the company on the losing end of that sentence. I spent yesterday checking whether the claim holds up, and my read is that it is probably true and much smaller than it sounds.

## What Huawei actually claimed

DigiTimes reported on Thursday that Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, said the company's Ascend accelerators have moved ahead of Nvidia in China on both sales and market share. The Register had the same claim on Wednesday. Xu made the remarks at a media roundtable during Huawei Connect in Shanghai on September 17, and he added a caveat most of the coverage skipped: reliable figures on Nvidia's share inside China are hard to collect, so the comparison rests on Huawei's own books. There is real money behind it. Tom's Hardware reported that Huawei expects roughly 12 billion US dollars in AI processor revenue this year, up from 7.5 billion last year, on orders already placed by Alibaba, ByteDance and Tencent. Reuters reported on September 16 that Huawei cannot build the chips fast enough to fill the orders it has.

## Nvidia's side of the ledger is empty

Nvidia is barely in this market to lose it. Jensen Huang has said the company's share of China's AI chip market fell from about 95 per cent to zero, and when Nvidia guided to 108 billion dollars of revenue for its fiscal third quarter in late August, the forecast carried a footnote saying it assumes no data centre compute revenue from China at all. The H200 was supposed to fix that. Washington authorized those sales last December, and roughly ten Chinese firms, Alibaba and Tencent and ByteDance among them, hold licences for up to 75,000 units each. Not one chip has shipped. American rules require the chips stay inside China, while Beijing has told its own companies to keep Nvidia hardware offshore and buy domestic at home. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told Bloomberg that semiconductor controls were not even on the agenda at the Trump and Xi summit on September 24.

## Market share is not compute

Here is where I part ways with the headline. The Council on Foreign Relations published an analysis last December comparing both roadmaps, and found the best American AI chips are about five times more powerful than Huawei's best, with that gap widening to seventeen times by 2027. Huawei's own published roadmap has the Ascend 950PR and 950DT, both due this year, delivering less total processing power than the Ascend 910C it already sells. The production math is worse. Even on aggressive assumptions, the CFR analysis put Huawei at roughly 5 per cent of Nvidia's aggregate AI computing power in 2025, 4 per cent this year and 2 per cent in 2027. SemiAnalysis has argued the binding constraint is **HBM**, the stacked high bandwidth memory that sits next to the processor and feeds it data, which China still cannot produce at volume.

## The takeaway

Watch whether a single H200 actually crosses the border, because one shipment would tell you whether the deadlock between Washington and Beijing is policy or posture. Watch Chinese HBM output too, since that caps Ascend volumes no matter how good Huawei's order book looks. If you are a Canadian taxpayer, Ottawa's 2 billion dollar Sovereign AI Compute Strategy is spending on data centres and public supercomputing, so whatever gets racked here is priced by this fight. The number on my own watchlist comes from CNBC on September 26: Chinese open models were 57 to 67 per cent of tokens used on the developer platform OpenRouter in the week of September 14, up from 6 to 13 per cent in February, so China can lose the chip race and still set the defaults.
